source.title: Implicit Regularization and Generalization in Overparameterized Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Text includes the full paper, including methods, results, discussion, limitations, and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: Reports controlled experiments on width, batch size, and optimizer that bear on claim versions, using this study's model and training configurations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on model width, batch size, optimizer, loss geometry, NTK movement, and pruning. Only results that measure the behaviors named by V2, V4, or V5 are included as rows. The loss geometry measures are not magnitude-aware sharpness as specified by V7. Cited findings from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures test performance across network widths, optimizers and batch sizes, bearing on V2, V4 and V5 with different architectures and training configurations from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' main interpretation: optimization dynamics, model scale and loss geometry jointly influence generalization. The authors also claim double descent, movement toward NTK behavior and lottery-ticket effects. Their claims of strict batch-size monotonicity and an 8-channel CNN interpolation threshold overstate their tables: batch 256 slightly outperforms 128, and the 8-channel CNN reaches only 45.8% training accuracy. The MNIST table shows continued improvement after interpolation but no preceding test-error peak. The authors acknowledge that the proposed causal links are not established.
record.recipe_differences: Controlled computational study of four-layer MLPs and CNNs on MNIST and CIFAR-10; it varies width and optimizer/batch conditions rather than reproducing the original studies' specific methods and settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test accuracy and generalization gap vary with batch size; model width changes test accuracy, including a dip near interpolation; Adam differs from SGD in the tested configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: The small-batch CNN has a lower top Hessian eigenvalue and smaller loss increases under absolute Gaussian weight perturbations than the large-batch CNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled local curvature and absolute perturbation sensitivity covary with test accuracy in this two-model comparison; this does not test V7's magnitude-aware measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Table VI reports decreasing relative parameter movement and increasing test accuracy with width on a separate MNIST subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider networks move less relative to initialization and improve held-out accuracy; absent training-fit measurements, this experiment does not establish improvement after interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Magnitude-pruned subnetworks retain much of the full model's accuracy, and original initialization outperforms random reinitialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse subnetworks can retain predictive performance, with initialization affecting retraining success; this concerns weights rather than V8's memorized examples.

record.problems: The paper tests a limited set of architectures and datasets; its MNIST double-descent subset has 10,000 training samples. The CIFAR-10 CNN sweep has very high reported variability at 8 channels. No random-label capacity check is reported. The loss-geometry analysis is on two models and does not establish causality; the paper itself says causal relationships cannot be confirmed from observational experiments alone.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded the full-batch GD row because it used a 5,000-sample subset and reached only 36.7% training accuracy, so it is not a matched batch-size result for V5. Excluded Hessian, perturbation, NTK, and lottery-ticket results because they do not measure a behavior named by V1–V8 as written. No other width or batch-sweep rows were omitted.

untested.parts: No random-label training or random-label held-out evaluation.

No one-hidden-layer replication or downsampled CIFAR-10 experiment; training uses finite epoch budgets without establishing convergence at every width. The MNIST results do not show an interpolation-associated test-error peak.
No matched image-task comparison between convolutional and fully connected architectures, local-connectivity intervention or transferred initialization.
No reported tuning search, language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay or optimizer switching.
No longer-training comparison, warmup intervention, normalization or regularization intervention, or language-model experiment.
No magnitude-scaled perturbation measure, perturbation tolerance based on training error, or comparison of gap rankings against norm and margin measures.
No identification and removal of memorized training examples; parameter pruning measures a different intervention.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. No verdict uses the confounded full-batch control. Reported uncertainties are standard deviations across five seeds; relevant pairwise significance results are not supplied. The CNN width sweep and optimizer experiment report markedly different accuracies for the same nominal 32-channel architecture, 65.8% and 84.72%; experiment-specific training details do not fully resolve this discrepancy. These experiments should be compared within their respective tables.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or held-out evaluation on random labels.
Uses a four-layer MLP and a CNN, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks; no downsampled CIFAR-10 experiment.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks on the same image task.
Tests Adam against SGD on one CIFAR-10 CNN configuration only; no language benchmarks, broader tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Tests batch sizes on one CIFAR-10 CNN for 80 epochs; no language models, alternative epoch budgets, or normalization and regularization changes.
Measures Hessian eigenvalues and absolute Gaussian weight perturbations, not magnitude-aware sharpness or rankings against norm- and margin-based measures.
